Are investors' hopes for a Fed "market bailout" doomed to disappoint? Despite warnings from Wall Street and the Treasury, strong economic data and persistently rising inflationary pressures are pushing the Fed to stick with its 25-basis-point rate hike next month.

The Fed's hawkish stance and readiness to raise rates again in December have dashed the hopes of investors battered by market volatility.Although most traders had bet on a 25-basis-point rate hike next month, the sharp stock market fluctuations have altered market expectations for the pace of subsequent rate hikes.

In September, the Fed raised its target interest rate to 3.75% to 4% to address soaring fuel prices triggered by the conflict between Trump and Iran. While the Fed chose to hold rates steady in October, the September rate hike and expectations of further tightening in December have led to tighter financial conditions and a stronger dollar, thereby depressing import prices.

With international oil prices falling, the necessity for a significant 50-basis-point rate hike by the Fed in December has been eliminated.

**Officials, while aware that a collapse in AI trading could impact the economy, still insist on a further 25 basis point rate hike, given that the 2% inflation target has been missed for nearly six consecutive years.** **Strong Data and AI Inflation Spillover Reinforce Hawkish Stance** **Official data released Wednesday showed that the Fed's preferred inflation gauge rose slightly to 3.8% in October. Excluding volatile food and energy prices, the core personal consumption expenditures price index, considered a better measure of underlying price pressures, accelerated its year-on-year increase to 3.3% from 3.1%.** **Another report released on the same day showed that the U.S. economy grew at an annualized rate of 4.3% in the third quarter, significantly higher than the 2.2% in the second quarter.** **The White House also announced a new round of tariffs on Wednesday, meaning the effects of Trump's tariffs on pushing up prices may continue to manifest.** The Federal Reserve is currently taking a hawkish stance, with officials concerned that high economic growth, partly driven by the artificial intelligence boom, coupled with a strong labor market, could entangle inflation above its target level. The AI ​​boom is driving up prices for goods beyond computer chips and software, a phenomenon that has alarmed the central bank. Chicago Fed President John Goolsby, who will have a vote on monetary policy in 2027, told reporters last week that he sees worrying signs of inflation "outside of the data center sector." Goolsby revealed, "We're hearing a lot of feedback like, 'My God, construction costs are incredibly high,' especially for any electrical components. Prices for anything similar to what's used in data centers are skyrocketing." Harvard professor Gita Gopinath previously worked with Fed Chairman Walsh on a panel of thirty. She pointed out, "Wash mentioned after the last Fed rate decision that we were entering an information-intensive period. Almost everything released since then points to the need for action—the only thing going in the opposite direction is risk sentiment." Technology Stock Plunge Triggers Warnings from Wall Street and the Treasury Since October, the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index has plummeted, erasing most of its year-to-date gains. There are widespread concerns that rising borrowing costs will dampen the spending spree in the artificial intelligence sector. On Monday, Nvidia reinstated its scandal-ridden CEO, Jensen Huang, briefly boosting tech stocks and easing fears of a market crash. However, the sell-off returned later in the week, with both the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite closing lower on Wednesday before Thanksgiving. Fears of sudden liquidations in AI trading have prompted economists, market participants, and even Treasury Secretary Bessant to call on the Fed to pause rate hikes in December. Bessant believes that hawkish comments from some central bank officials are part of the reason for the stock market decline. In an interview with CBS News last Sunday, Bessant said, "Many people believe that if they tighten too much, they might make a policy mistake." Hedge fund manager Ackman also claimed on social media this week that if the Fed continues to raise interest rates, it will "drag the U.S. and the world into recession." Torsten Sløk, chief economist at Apollo Global Management, pointed out, "If they look at inflation, they should raise rates. But if they look at the prospects for artificial intelligence, they should probably cut rates." He believes that the recent market turmoil is a strong reason to remain very cautious about raising interest rates.

Faced with market sentiment fluctuating wildly with individual stocks, Eric Wallerstein, chief macro strategist at Clocktower Group and former advisor to former Federal Reserve Governor Milan, bluntly stated: "People's interest rate expectations are completely dictated by Nvidia's stock price, which doesn't seem like the proper way to formulate monetary policy."

The Absence of "Fed Put Options" Tests Warsh's Determination

However, traders hoping for Fed intervention to rescue the market may have underestimated Warsh's determination to curb inflation. Guy Miller, chief market strategist at Zurich Insurance Group, said: "The kind of 'Fed put options' that could have supported the market in the past years no longer exist."

The so-called "Fed put options" refer to the market belief formed during former Fed Chairman Greenspan's tenure, namely, that investors believed the central bank would prop up the market by providing cheap funds when the stock market falters.

Claudia Sahm, chief economist at New Century Advisors, also believes that the Fed will not change course in the short term due to a stock market correction.

She stated, "At this juncture, it's difficult to get them to abandon their focus on inflation. For the stock market to force the Fed to change its stance, the decline would need to be much larger."

data.title: Is it still a good time to buy the dip before Thanksgiving? US stocks and cryptocurrencies are all on sale.
data.description:
Author: Jae, PANews

On November 25th, just one day before Thanksgiving in the United States, Wall Street did not experience the expected pre-holiday relaxation.

The S&P 500 plunged as much as 3.2% during the day, and the Nasdaq once fell by more than 4%. After a wave of panic selling, bargain hunters entered the market at the end of the day, and the two major indices ultimately closed down 0.25% and 0.62% respectively, staging a dramatic V-shaped reversal. During the same period, Bitcoin fluctuated around $60,000, gold fell below its lowest level in more than a year, and the US dollar hovered near its highest level this year.

On November 25th, just one day before Thanksgiving in the United States, Wall Street did not experience the expected relaxation.

This year's Thanksgiving holiday coincided with a period of inflationary risks, tariff frictions, tech stock revaluation, and capital flight. The holiday rally, traditionally seen as a catalyst for year-end gains, seems to be losing its magic. The US stock market's Thanksgiving rally is ahead of schedule; the "Black Friday rally" is no longer effective. While the Thanksgiving rally isn't as famous as the "Santa Claus rally" in the US stock market's holiday history, it still has a respectable track record. According to Exent statistics, in 53 out of 76 years from 1950 to 2025, the S&P 500 recorded gains during Thanksgiving week, with an average increase of about 0.7% and a median increase of 0.87%. Data from Morgan Stanley's E*TRADE also confirms this, showing that since 1960, the median return during Thanksgiving week has been about three times that of other trading weeks. "Black Friday" is also a perennial winner. Historically, the S&P 500 has risen on Black Friday with a 71.1% probability. But if you zoom in, the story changes. Over the 20 years from 2006 to 2025, the probability of a price increase on Black Friday has fallen to 50%, and the median increase has turned negative to -0.04%, essentially no different from flipping a coin. With the popularization of algorithmic trading, the increased speed of information dissemination, and a deeper understanding of holiday patterns in the market, "holiday gains" are being increasingly eroded by early-mover funds. IG Group points out that the gains before and after Thanksgiving are mainly concentrated on the Wednesday before the holiday: 37 times in 50 years, with an average daily increase of 0.26%, maintaining a 70% success rate in the last 20 years. The Monday after the holiday is the most likely day for short-term traders to make mistakes, with only 19 gains in 50 years, and only 5 gains in the last 20 years, averaging a 0.32% decline per day, a typical weak day. This year, the "starting line" for Thanksgiving market movements has been moved even earlier. Before Thanksgiving week, the S&P 500 had fallen 8.83% in the month, a 11.62% pullback from its all-time high on October 6. Historically, when a significant decline has occurred in November, the probability of an increase during Thanksgiving week is only 50%. If the market has just pulled back more than 5% from its three-month high, the probability of an increase drops to 33.3%. On Monday, November 23, the market staged a violent rebound, with the S&P 500 surging 4.73% in a single day. Even with two consecutive days of decline, by the close of trading on November 25, the Thanksgiving week had still accumulated a gain of approximately 3.94%, far exceeding the historical average. In other words, this year's "Thanksgiving rally" has actually already occurred, but it's closer to a recovery after a deep correction than a healthy rally in the traditional sense. Hedge funds have withdrawn for five consecutive weeks, while retail investors have poured hundreds of billions into bottom-fishing. Pre-holiday market sentiment was far more divided than historical data suggests, with fast-moving and slow-moving money in the US stock market showing the most significant trading divergence in recent years. Vincent Lin, co-head of Goldman Sachs' Prime Insights and Analytics, revealed that hedge fund clients have reduced their overall risk exposure for five consecutive weeks while continuing to increase their short positions in individual stocks, index futures, and ETFs. Goldman Sachs estimates that quantitative trend funds (CTAs) will mechanically sell between $28.6 billion and $80.6 billion next week, regardless of market performance. In stark contrast to institutional risk-cutting is the continued influx of retail funds. Over the past month, US stock ETFs and mutual funds have attracted approximately $150 billion in inflows. This long-term optimistic outlook is also reflected in the year-end forecasts of Wall Street investment banks. On November 25th, Deutsche Bank announced an optimistic target of 9,000 points for the S&P 500 by the end of 2027, while Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley both aimed for 8,700 points, and even the relatively cautious JPMorgan Chase gave a forecast of 8,200 points. However, the VIX volatility index hovered around 27, significantly higher than its long-term median of 17.6, and the VIX futures curve remained inverted, indicating that market apprehension about short-term risks had not dissipated. On one hand, hedge funds significantly reduced their positions to mitigate risk before the holiday; on the other hand, retail investors and top investment banks were confident in their bullish narratives for next year. Thanksgiving is like a transition point between capital and emotions, simultaneously presenting the market with short-term panic and long-term confidence. The Bitcoin "dinner party" approach fails, and liquidity follows Wall Street into holiday mode. A story circulates in the crypto market: Americans gather around the dinner table during the holiday to introduce Bitcoin to family and friends, thus bringing in a new group of potential buyers. This narrative was particularly prevalent in 2017, when Bitcoin entered a phase of large-scale public dissemination. According to SimianX statistics, in the 15 Thanksgiving weeks from 2011 to 2025, Bitcoin rose 9 times, with an average increase of 4.4% and a median of 4.9%. The 2013 Thanksgiving week saw a dramatic 40.6% increase, pushing the holiday effect to its peak. However, as Bitcoin has evolved from a geek experiment into a global financial asset, this pattern has largely become invalid. In the past 10 years, the probability of Bitcoin rising during Thanksgiving week has dropped to 40%, and the average return has reversed to -0.73%. The long-term average returns, initially inflated by extreme market conditions, have gradually lost their reference value. The real window of opportunity for Bitcoin may actually be hidden after the holidays. Over the past five years, Bitcoin has seen five consecutive weeks of gains following holidays. More noteworthy than price patterns is the structural change in trading rhythm. In the past, the crypto market operated 24/7, and holidays were actually times when retail trading was more active and trading volume increased. CoinQuant data shows that Bitcoin trading volume during Thanksgiving was generally higher than usual from 2017 to 2021. However, from 2022 to 2025, holiday trading volume has been lower than usual for four consecutive years, averaging a decrease of about 31.3%. Kaiko data also shows that the percentage of Bitcoin trading volume over weekends has decreased from 28% in 2019 to 16% in 2024. Institutional investors, spot ETFs, and professional market makers are playing an increasingly important role, and the trading clock in the crypto market is aligning with that of the US stock market. With Wall Street closed for holidays, liquidity in the crypto market is also shrinking. Short-term uncertainty stems from options settlement. Deribit, the world's largest crypto options exchange, will see approximately 111,800 Bitcoin monthly options settle on Black Friday, releasing nearly half of its negative Gamma exposure. Glassnode warns that in the negative Gamma zone, market makers may be forced to chase highs and lows to maintain Delta neutrality, leading to potentially sharp short-term fluctuations. Pressure also remains on the spot market. Cooling buying in DAT (Digital Asset Treasury), continued outflows of Wall Street institutional funds from ETFs, and widening losses for short-term holders mean that even without large-scale liquidations, prices may continue to be under pressure. Holiday Effect Takes a Backseat: Gold Bulls and Bears Clash, Dollar Faces Year-End Headwinds

Compared to US stocks and Bitcoin, the Thanksgiving performance of gold and the US dollar is more driven by interest rate expectations and year-end fund reallocation, with the holiday effect being a secondary variable.

FOREX.com market analyst Matt Simpson points out that gold typically performs relatively well on the Tuesday before Thanksgiving and the Friday after, with probabilities of rising of 58.9% and 61.5% respectively.

However, the holiday pattern for gold is generally weak.

According to GoldInvestor statistics, COMEX gold futures have risen in 11 out of the past 20 Thanksgiving weeks and fallen in 9, a success rate of 55%, with an average price fluctuation of only about 2%, showing almost no significant one-sided tendency. The gold market in the past month has been caught in a tug-of-war between its safe-haven and monetary attributes. Trade frictions, geopolitical conflicts, and the sell-off in tech stocks theoretically benefit safe-haven demand, but rebounding inflation, expectations of interest rate hikes, and high real interest rates are continuously raising the opportunity cost of holding gold. The divergence between bulls and bears is now on the table. On November 24th, Roukaya Ibrahim, one of Wall Street's most steadfast gold bulls and chief commodity strategist at BCA Research, announced the end of his four-year long gold trade, citing the possibility of the US dollar index potentially surging towards 105 in the short term, high real yields, and the risk of a correction in gold ETF holdings. A day later, gold fell below $3,500 intraday, hitting a new low since September of last year. Bridgewater Associates founder Ray Dalio publicly stated that in an era of high debt and escalating trade conflicts, allocating 10%-15% of an investment portfolio to gold remains irreplaceable, and central banks are pushing gold to the position of the world's second-largest currency. Institutional target prices also showed a divergent trend. Goldman Sachs lowered its year-end 2026 target to $4,150, UBS maintained its target at $4,500, and Morgan Stanley listed gold as its top pick for 2027 in its annual outlook released in November. The holiday pattern for the US dollar is more pronounced. FOREX.com data shows that since 1985, the US dollar index has consistently recorded negative returns in the three days leading up to Thanksgiving, with a less than 50% probability of rising. According to StoneX statistics, since 2000, the US dollar index has fallen 20 times from Thanksgiving to the end of the year, with an average decline of 1.08%, making year-end weakness a high-probability event. This year, the US dollar is also caught in a tug-of-war between two forces. Interest rate hike expectations provided support, while a cooling AI industry and growth concerns drove funds into long-term bonds, lowering long-term interest rates and weakening the dollar's interest rate advantage. On November 25th, the yield on the 10-year US Treasury note fell 6.2 basis points to 4.84%, and the dollar index fell 0.14%. OCBC Bank FX strategist Sim Moh Siong believes that the risk-reward ratio for continuing to chase the dollar has decreased. Conclusion: Wall Street is never short of holiday stories. From Thanksgiving rallies to Santa Claus rallies, investors always try to find repeatable patterns in the chaotic market to add some certainty to their trading. However, historical data is ultimately just probability, and the holiday effect doesn't always materialize as expected every year. This year's Thanksgiving is particularly true. The variables that truly determine market direction—AI trading revaluation, inflation stickiness, tariff risks, and institutional deleveraging—don't stop evolving just because traders are on holiday. During the relatively illiquid holiday period, the true market trend may only begin to emerge after market participants return on November 30th.

data.title: RWA enters the era of "major infrastructure".
data.description:
Written by: imToken

On November 19, 2026, Anthropic officially listed on Nasdaq with an offering price of $83 per share. This highly anticipated IPO of the AI ​​giant not only became the focus of traditional capital markets but also a real-world stress test for the crypto market.

Even before the listing, the price of Anthropic Pre-IPO contracts on OKX once surged to approximately 103 USDC, a premium of about 24% over the offering price. After the official listing, several crypto trading platforms quickly followed suit, launching corresponding tokenized stock products, allowing on-chain users to directly access the hottest assets in traditional capital markets.

This is also an interesting microcosm; since 2025, from traditional US exchanges to crypto trading platforms, and to financial regulatory agencies around the world, a competition surrounding RWA infrastructure has been unfolding.

I. Does RWA Bring Incremental Funds or Divert Existing Capital? In the past, RWA was largely seen as a bridge connecting traditional finance and crypto. From US Treasury bonds and money market funds to gold, private credit, and now listed stocks and equity in unlisted companies, more and more traditional assets are entering the on-chain world in tokenized form. The Anthropic case is quite representative. In the traditional system, investors participating in a company's IPO typically need to go through multiple hurdles, including brokerage accounts, investor qualification reviews, and subscription allocation. However, the pre-IPO and tokenized stocks of crypto platforms allow users to directly participate in trading with stablecoins, eliminating the need for funds in traditional securities accounts. Some products even support 24/7 trading. It's fair to say that tokenized stocks have visibly grown into a substantial market over the past year. A CoinGecko November 2026 report shows that as of October 21, the total market capitalization of tokenized stocks had increased from $1.25 billion in July to $2.71 billion, with an average daily trading volume of approximately $402 million. This doesn't include the trading volume of derived perpetual contracts. However, market expansion does not equate to a corresponding increase in new funds for crypto. While these assets do provide new allocation outlets for idle on-chain funds and have the potential to attract some investors accustomed to traditional brokerage systems to crypto platforms, funds may also flow out of existing DeFi lending, liquidity mining, and native crypto asset trading, shifting towards tokenized bonds, money market funds, and equity products. In other words, RWA brings not only incremental expansion but also a redistribution of existing capital structures. According to Binance Research, the current capital activation rate of on-chain RWA remains limited. After tokenization, a large number of assets are still primarily used for holding and trading, and have not yet fully entered more complex financial applications such as lending, staking, and portfolio investment. This also means that the real problem RWA needs to solve in the next stage is how to ensure the continuous flow of these assets on-chain and generate more financial activities. If the demand for RWA mainly comes from existing crypto market participants, its growth may be more reflected in the reallocation of existing capital. The ability to continuously attract external capital and expand on-chain financial applications will be an important dimension for measuring the long-term value of RWA. II. Competition over Infrastructure from Asset Issuance to Transaction Settlement If the early RWA project addressed "how to put assets on the blockchain," the current competitive focus has shifted to who can control the core hubs of issuance, ownership confirmation, trading, clearing, and fund settlement. This has led to the entry of traditional financial giants, cryptocurrency exchanges, and retail brokerages, resulting in a rapidly diverging landscape with three clear paths. 1. NYSE and ICE: Bringing the Traditional Securities Market "Natively" On-Chain In January 2026, the NYSE's parent company, Intercontinental Exchange (ICE), announced the development of a tokenized securities trading platform, planning to support 24-hour trading, fractional share trading, and instant settlement for US-listed stocks and ETFs, and allowing the use of stablecoins for fund settlement. The core idea is to combine the NYSE's existing Pillar matching engine with a blockchain-based post-trade processing, settlement, and custody system. It supports both "tokenized shares interchangeable with traditional stocks" and "natively issued digital securities," a fundamental difference from common price-tracking tokens—holders will continue to enjoy the dividends and corporate governance rights corresponding to real shares. On November 2nd, the NYSE further announced its transfer agent partners, including Securitize, tZERO, Superstate, and traditional giants such as Broadridge, Computershare, and Equiniti. This indicates that TradFi is connecting existing issuer relationships, shareholder registration, and securities services systems with blockchain infrastructure. 2. OKX and ICE: A Two-Track Extension of Crypto Trading Platforms In contrast to the NYSE's extension from traditional to on-chain, OKX represents a two-way exploration by crypto platforms towards traditional securities entry points. One route is the compliance infrastructure route. In June 2026, OKX and ICE established a joint venture, OKXICE, and submitted a trading venue plan to the U.S. SEC in October. OKXICE officially launched its tokenized securities trading venue on November 23, 2026. Another approach is product distribution targeting existing crypto users. The Unified Tokenized Stocks, launched in November, integrates similar stocks from different issuers under the xStocks framework into a unified order book and corporate action rules. It supports 24-hour USDT trading and withdrawals to the Solana and X Layer networks. However, these products currently do not grant actual equity or voting rights to the underlying companies; they are essentially primarily providing price exposure. 3. Robinhood: Brokerage Entry Point, Integrating On-Chain Finance As a securities brokerage with a large retail base, Robinhood has chosen a more front-end entry point strategy. In July 2026, it launched a new generation of Stock Tokens through its Jersey subsidiary—essentially tokenized debt securities where the issuer buys and holds the corresponding underlying securities as collateral. Holders do not obtain legal ownership or shareholder rights of the underlying stocks. With the ongoing development of Robinhood Wallet and on-chain infrastructure, Robinhood's advantage lies not in reinventing the wheel, but in packaging its existing securities business, user distribution capabilities, and on-chain financial services into a unified entry point. After all, it already possesses a large stock investor base and a mature financial services system. In summary, each of the three paths has its own objectives: traditional exchanges aim for control over issuance, registration, and clearing; crypto platforms attempt to introduce stablecoins, global traffic, and 24/7 trading to traditional assets; and fintech brokers aim to integrate brokerage, wallets, and on-chain entry points. However, increased entrants do not automatically lead to unified liquidity in the market. On the contrary, shares of the same company may now exist on multiple issuance platforms, multiple public chains, and different trading venues, with each issuing entity, legal structure, custody arrangements, and redemption mechanism being incompatible. This is a problem that requires long-term solutions. III. Regulatory Boundaries: RWA Development Cannot Bypass the Fundamental Rules of the Financial Market The development of RWA involves not only technology and business models, but also securities issuance, asset ownership verification, investor protection, and cross-border capital flows. From the current regulatory dynamics, different regions are exploring different institutional paths, but one fundamental principle is becoming increasingly clear—asset tokenization does not automatically change the legal attributes of the underlying assets. As long as a token substantially corresponds to securities rights, it must return to the constraints of the corresponding financial rules. Regulatory changes in the United States are worth noting. On September 17, 2026, the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) issued a temporary, conditional exemption mechanism for tokenized securities trading venues, known as the Innovation Exemption. This allows eligible tokenized securities venues to trade certain U.S.-listed stocks through licensed automated market makers and liquidity pools under specific conditions, without having to register as exchanges in the traditional way. However, the exemption does not mean a relaxation of all regulatory requirements. The SEC has imposed several restrictions, including limitations on the types and sizes of tokenized stocks that can be traded; holders must enjoy the same rights as traditional shareholders of the same class; for third-party tokenized stocks, the issuer of the underlying securities must be provided with the opportunity to notify and raise objections; and smart contracts must be publicly auditable, among others. This reflects the U.S. regulatory authorities' attempt to integrate blockchain trading into the existing securities market regulatory framework. In contrast, the regulatory attitude in mainland China is more cautious. On February 6, 2026, eight departments, including the People's Bank of China, the National Development and Reform Commission, and the China Securities Regulatory Commission, jointly issued the "Notice on Further Preventing and Handling Risks Related to Virtual Currencies" (Yinfa [2026] No. 42), which for the first time clearly defined the tokenization of real-world assets and reiterated that conducting RWA tokenization activities and related intermediary and technical services within China is suspected of being illegal financial activities and should be prohibited—only reserving an exception for businesses "conducted with the consent of the competent business authorities in accordance with laws and regulations and relying on specific financial infrastructure." On the same day, the China Securities Regulatory Commission also issued the "Regulatory Guidelines on the Issuance of Asset-Backed Securities Tokens Overseas by Domestic Assets," establishing clear filing thresholds: for any issuance of related tokens overseas with domestic asset cash flow as repayment support, the domestic entity actually controlling the underlying assets must file with the China Securities Regulatory Commission and submit complete materials, while strictly complying with regulations on cross-border investment, foreign exchange management, and network data security; any activity not approved, filed, or subject to security review is prohibited. Hong Kong, under a separate financial regulatory framework, is accelerating the transition of tokenized finance from pilot programs to real-world business transactions. On October 26, 2026, the Hong Kong Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) approved the first two tokenized money market funds to conduct 24/7 secondary market trading on licensed virtual asset trading platforms. On November 2, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) announced a new phase for Project Ensemble, supporting 24/7 interbank settlement of tokenized deposits using tokenized central bank currency, with the number of participating banks increasing to 12 and industry institutions to 20. As emphasized by the HKMA and SFC in a joint event in November, Hong Kong's tokenized market is moving from the experimental stage to commercialization, with the next phase focusing on generating real business flows between tokenized investment products, digital currencies, and financial infrastructure. In conclusion, looking back at the development of RWA, a clear shift emerges. Initially, the industry focused on mapping real-world assets onto the blockchain, allowing government bonds, gold, real estate, and stocks to exist as tokens. Subsequently, the market explored how to facilitate asset trading through stablecoins, distribute profits through smart contracts, and introduce tokenized assets into DeFi lending and collateral systems. Now, with giants like the NYSE, ICE, OKX, and Robinhood making moves, competition has penetrated into the heart of the financial market, encompassing issuance, registration, custody, trading, and clearing. For wallets, this means their future responsibilities may extend beyond simply managing private keys and displaying on-chain assets. When users begin to access tokenized stocks, funds, and other real-world assets through wallets, wallets need to help users identify the asset issuer, underlying equity, custody arrangements, redemption mechanisms, and transfer restrictions, enabling users to truly understand what they are holding. In this sense, RWA not only brings more tradable assets to crypto, but also drives the entire industry to rethink the relationship between wallets, payments, trading, and asset management.

data.title: The disruptive applications of AI: still hidden in the corners
data.description:
Recently, at the APEC summit, Lei Jun, when discussing the current development of AI, mentioned (paraphrased):

The development of large-scale AI models has been rapid over the past four years, but industry investment is large, application scenarios are limited, and few companies have achieved profitability. He pointed out the harsh challenges that current AI development brings to enterprises.

In the various AI fields I understand, currently, apart from a very few application areas (such as ByteDance's Red Fruit short dramas) and hardware and contract manufacturing companies (such as Nvidia, TSMC, and some component companies), many companies are forced into an arms race that they have no choice but to participate in, investing heavily but seeing no returns in the short term.

Even top large-scale model companies (such as Anthropic) have achieved amazing revenue growth in their enterprise-facing businesses, but this is still a drop in the ocean compared to the computing power expenditures they will have to invest in the future. It will take some time for revenue to fully cover expenses and achieve a completely positive cash flow.

The substantial profits of already profitable hardware and contract manufacturing companies are also driven by the expected expenditures of large-scale model companies.

Large-scale model companies dare to invest heavily because they have seen the potential of superintelligence, especially in mathematics, physics, and biology. Under such extremely attractive expectations, the entire industry, especially the capital market, is willing to pay for such extravagant spending. In some areas that have generated positive cash flow, although individual applications (such as Red Fruit Short Drama) appear to have generated cash flow, the vast majority of short video creators in the entire field are still losing money. Therefore, this profit model may not be easily replicated or imitated by other companies. Furthermore, I believe that for AI, a disruptive technology, short videos are certainly not disruptive applications. Essentially, they only upgrade and improve the efficiency of the existing (video) industry, without changing the industry's production relations and profit distribution relationships. Therefore, this application is likely only temporary and may be replaced and disrupted by new AI video applications in the future. Overall, in the current AI ecosystem, what people are most confident in and certain of is the foundation of the entire ecosystem—large-scale models and related hardware supply chains. It not only determines the foundation for the future growth of a country/ecosystem, but also its very lifeline. Therefore, capital from all sectors is pouring into this field, whether actively or passively. This reminds me of the early development of the crypto ecosystem: After Ethereum launched in 2015, the following two years saw the value and potential of smart contract public chains. Thus, in the ICO boom of 2017, the vast majority of projects, especially those with astonishing funding, were smart contract public chains. These projects aimed to create Ethereum killers, aiming to monopolize the foundation of the entire ecosystem. At that time, ecosystem participants paid little attention to application areas, nor were they able to. This was not only because people couldn't see any specific application areas that could generate real-world applications and revenue; it was also because people were convinced that once they secured dominance in the smart contract public chain foundation, they could share in the monopolistic profits regardless of any future applications. However, that fierce competition for funding ultimately ended in disaster, with 99.99% of ICO public chains failing. Conversely, peripheral applications, which had been relatively inconspicuous during the subsequent bear market, became the leaders of the DeFi boom and the infrastructure for applications across the entire crypto ecosystem today. This round of AI competition may follow a similar path, with most competitors focusing on large-scale models failing, leaving only a very few. Meanwhile, the currently inconspicuous peripheral applications may become giants and infrastructure in new application areas in the future.
